hook: Berries, greens and mushrooms by the month, the market's harvest, and the look-alikes that can kill
intro: The Northwest feeds anyone who knows where to look. Salmonberries ripen in May as the first fruit of the year, huckleberries cover the mountain slopes in August, and the autumn rains bring chanterelles up through the moss. People here have harvested camas, berries, shellfish and salmon for thousands of years.

It's also home to some of the most poisonous plants and mushrooms in North America, several of them easy to mistake for something good. Start with the berries and greens that have no dangerous double, learn one new food at a time, and never eat anything on the say-so of a website, this one included.
rules: Be completely sure. If you're not, leave it. A local mushroom club or a person who knows it in the field is worth more than any photo.
Take a little, from where there's a lot, and leave plenty for the birds, the bears and the next person.

Check the rules for the land: national forests usually allow picking for your own use within limits (some need a free permit); national and state parks often limit amounts or forbid it; tribal and private land needs permission.
Stay away from roadsides, sprayed fields and polluted water.
Shellfish need a licence in Washington and Oregon, and seaweed does in Washington. Shellfish beaches close for toxins: check the closures the same day you go.

wild.note: The first berry of the year, gold to deep red, along streams and in clearings.
Tiny and intense, on open slopes and trail edges.
Bright red, tart, on bushes growing from old stumps in the lowland forest.
Soft, shallow red caps under big maple-like leaves.
Serviceberry: purple, sweet and seedy, on the drier east side and in the gorge.
The native trailing blackberry: smaller and better than the invader.
The mountain huckleberry, the great berry of the Cascades, on old burns and subalpine slopes.
Himalayan blackberry is invasive: pick all you like.
Salal: dark, mealy and sweet, good in jam.
Blue elderberry, cooked only. Its red cousin is the one to avoid.
wild.dangerNote: Red elderberry's raw berries, seeds, stems and leaves are toxic.

wild.note: Evergreen huckleberry: small, shiny and black, on the coast into November.
Oregon grape: very sour; best in jelly or with sweeter fruit.
Young tops, picked with gloves and cooked or dried; cooking takes away the sting.
Miner's lettuce: mild and juicy, in damp shade in spring.
Redwood sorrel: lemony leaves, a few at a time (they hold oxalic acid).
Lady fern fiddleheads, cooked. Not bracken, whose shoots are carcinogenic.
Nodding onion: it smells of onion. Anything onion-like that doesn't is not.
wild.dangerNote: Death camas grows in the same meadows, has no onion smell, and kills.

wild.note: Common camas was a staple food here for thousands of years; leave the digging to those whose tradition it is, and enjoy the blue meadows.
wild.dangerNote: Death camas has creamy white flowers but identical bulbs, and grows among the camas.

wild.note: Beaked hazelnut: pick before the squirrels, as the husks turn brown.
Spruce tips in spring, bright and citrusy, for tea or syrup.
Morels come up in spring, often the year after a forest fire. Always cooked.
wild.dangerNote: False morels have lobed, brain-like caps and are stuffed with cottony tissue, not hollow.

wild.note: Lobster mushroom: a mould that turns another mushroom bright orange and firm.
The Pacific golden chanterelle, Oregon's state mushroom: false gills like ridges, apricot smell.
wild.dangerNote: The false chanterelle has true, thin, forked gills and grows on wood; not deadly, but not good.

wild.note: King bolete: a sponge under the cap, not gills, and a fat, netted stem.
Matsutake: spicy cinnamon smell, under pine and hemlock.
wild.dangerNote: Smith's amanita looks much like matsutake, lacks the smell, and destroys the kidneys.

wild.note: Conifer coral hedgehog: white cascades of spines on old logs.
Yellowfoot: small, hollow, in mossy wet forest into winter.
Shaggy mane: cook within hours, before it melts into ink.
Bull kelp: young fronds and stipes; cut, don't pull the holdfast. A licence is needed in Washington.
Razor clams, on the surf beaches when the season opens; dates are set by the state each year.
Dungeness crab: seasons and size limits differ by area.

deadly.note: Western water hemlock, in wet ground, is the most poisonous plant in North America; a bite of root can kill. Leave every wild member of the carrot family alone.
Poison hemlock: tall, purple-blotched hollow stems, along roads and fields. Deadly.
The death cap, spreading in the Northwest under planted trees. Most mushroom deaths are from it.
Small and brown on rotting wood, with the same toxin as the death cap.
Baneberry: shiny red or white berries on a forest herb. Poisonous.
Green false hellebore, or corn lily, in wet mountain meadows. Highly toxic.
